events.excerpt: Working in tech support can be thankless when gormless colleagues leave you sleepless. Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script. He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP). "Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote. This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases. "In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the struct proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. events.excerpt: The ESP32-P4 is Espressif’s high-end application processor, with two blistering fast RISC-V cores for a surprisingly reasonable price. As it’s a very capable computer in its own right, there have been a range of operating systems made for it. Latest among them is [Jthwho]’s BMDS, for Bare Metal Do Stuff , which targets an Olimex board. At its heart is the FreeRTOS kernel we’ve seen in so many other similar projects, but on top is an OS which is described as being like DOS in its one-user minimally intrusive operation. It runs ELF binaries, and has some POSIX compliance, with BusyBox being a port. Perhaps most noticeable is its GUI, which provides a very slick desktop straight out of the late 1990s. We can see that had this appeared as a contemporary of Amigas, 68k Macs, and Windows 3.x, it would have immediately been a real contender. But the question is, does such an OS have a niche here in 2026? We think it might, as this processor is slowly establishing itself in a new genre of powerful machines aimed at hackers and tinkerers. Either way it’s an impressive achievement, and we look forward to seeing it develop over time.
events.headline: A Desktop OS for the ESP32-P4

Replacing customer funds doesn’t mean the stolen crypto is back, and US authorities are still pursuing it. Binance said on November 12 that it has finished replenishing every customer asset affected by the October 29 breach . It closed a shortfall of more than $6.34 billion with money from its corporate treasury, its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and its futures insurance fund. The exchange also published a new proof of reserves (PoR) snapshot covering 198 tokens, and once the matching zero-knowledge proof is generated, users will be able to confirm on their own that their balances are backed at least 1:1. The announcement came on the same day the US Department of Justice said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the stolen funds, which the FBI attributes to the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor. events.excerpt: Users of Microsoft 365 continued to experience service disruptions early Friday. At 2:14 a.m. UTC on November 13, Microsoft’s service-health dashboard continued to report service degradation for business and consumer products. The issues were not limited to Outlook. Other services, including Microsoft 365 Copilot and the Microsoft connectors utilized in systems like ChatGPT and Claude, were also affected. Shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, November 12, Outlook users started to complain about the loss of their connections. Later updates from Microsoft indicated that many of the affected services were dependent on Exchange Online. This explains why Teams chats and online meetings did continue to work, but scheduling meetings did not function properly at all. In addition, files that were saved in SharePoint were available. events.excerpt: On November 12, Tether, Tron, and Chainalysis formed a new alliance, known as the Digital Crime Task Force (DCTF) . It aims to identify illegal USDT transactions on the Tron blockchain and take preventive actions to block them before the money is moved. The DCTF comes after the dissolution of the T3 Financial Crime Unit, which was the combined venture of Tether, Tron, and TRM Labs, and was responsible for identifying more than $450 million worth of illegal transactions. Prompting the question: Will DCTF act faster than its predecessor? How the three-way handoff is supposed to work Every member of the alliance plays a specific role. Chainalysis uses blockchain data and AI-based tools to follow suspicious wallets. Tron assists investigators in tracing transactions on its blockchain. Tether, being the issuer of USDT, can freeze the funds of a flagged address. The DCTF will accept tips and requests to freeze assets from law enforcement. Its investigations will cover scams, hacks, North Korean cyber operations, and money laundering. Those investigations will focus on Tron, where more than $94 billion in USDT circulates. events.excerpt: North Korean hackers used accounts stolen from previous victims to invite new targets to video calls and played secretly recorded webcam clips of people those targets knew. The scheme, known as FaceStealer by the FBI, stole more than $400 million in crypto over 18 months, the Justice Department said Thursday. The department took down FaceStealer’s cloud infrastructure. The FBI also seized more than 900 webcam videos of the scheme’s victims under a federal warrant. DOJ says a fake audio glitch tricked targets into installing malware The DOJ said in a release that the crews target people working in crypto and web3. When a target joins, the hackers record that person’s own webcam and play back prerecorded footage of a known contact, faking the presence of a trusted colleague on the call. The hackers produce deepfake videos of influential people in crypto and web3 with what the department called “super intelligence,” and then run them in the same meetings. Partway through the call there is a bogus technical fault, for example that the target is not being heard. Then a link/prompt to “fix” it. It silently installs malware.
